The Afghanistan situation at the ICC dates back to November 2017, when then-prosecutor Fatou Bensouda first requested authorisation to investigate alleged crimes committed since 2003, including by Afghan and US forces as well as the Taliban and the IS-K group.
That request was initially rejected by a differently composed pre-trial chamber in 2019, before the appeals chamber overturned the decision in March 2020 and authorised the investigation to proceed.

"He was run over multiple times with his own vehicle," Yusuf's son, Mustafa Osman, told The Somali Brief.
Yusuf was reportedly found in a ditch nearly a mile away, suffering from broken legs and ribs, two collapsed lungs, a spinal injury and internal bleeding.
He remains hospitalised in a coma, according to his family.
Hopkins police confirmed that officers responding to a report of a suspicious vehicle at around 1.20am on Saturday discovered a seriously injured man and subsequently took a male suspect into custody.
According to the Times of India, arrest records show that a man identified as Samit Apurva Patel was taken into custody by Hopkins Police on 14 November on a first-degree assault charge.

In October, Malm was barred from entering the UK by the Home Office, and instead was set to appear by video link at the event for the magazine Tribune on 4 November at a venue owned by Hackney Council.
The event coincided with a legal challenge against the UK government’s controversial ban against Palestine Action which Ammori is fighting in the Supreme Court.

The disclosures reveal that an initial Home Office assessment found that the event was “unlikely to meet the threshold for disruption”.

Off
This year marked a quarter of a century since the beginning of the “war on terror”, and in that time, the British state has built one of the most extensive counter-extremism systems in the world.
Also this year, Britain produced - for the first time - an official definition of what it calls “anti-Muslim hostility”. It would be easy to treat these as separate stories, one about security and the other about community relations - but a new report from Cage International argues that they are not.
The definition has been shaped so precisely around the security state that, read closely, it functions less as a protection for Muslims than as a protection for the institutions that have spent two decades treating them as suspects.
The key, as the report sets out, lies in a single word that runs through every part of the definition: intent. Anti-Muslim hostility, as the government defines it, means intentionally engaging in criminal acts against Muslims, or stereotyping them “with the intention of encouraging hatred.” It means discrimination where the conduct “is intended to disadvantage Muslims in public and economic life”.
Discrimination rarely announces itself this way. The Islamophobia Response Unit, a charity that handles discrimination casework, has warned that the threshold excludes most of the cases it sees: bias, institutional barriers, and recruitment processes that quietly filter out applicants with Muslim names.

Iraq sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran group's bastion
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed nine officials on Saturday, following an investigation into allegations of oil smuggling in the Jurf al-Sakher area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group.
"In light of the investigation's findings," Zaidi "ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary," his military spokesman Sabah al-Numan said, without identifying the suspects.
The premier "also ordered the dismissal" of nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babylon province, an interior ministry commander, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the oil ministry.
Numan did not elaborate on the role of the sacked officials in the alleged smuggling operations.
A committee investigating the allegations entered Jurf al-Sakher on Friday, accompanied by members of Kataeb Hezbollah.
On Wednesday, the state news agency INA reported that "intelligence documents" containing satellite images "showed crude oil and oil-derivatives smuggling operations carried out by an armed faction" in Jurf al-Sakher, accusing the unnamed faction of tapping into a pipeline there.
According to Numan, the investigating committee "confirmed the accuracy" of the information.
Report by AFP

Trump may not attack Iran as long as it doesn't provoke US, report says
President Donald Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, according to three people familiar with the matter.
Trump has alternated between threats of escalating the war with new strikes and winding down hostilities, and current and former officials say he does not appear to have made up his mind about how to resolve the unpopular conflict, which he launched in February with Israel.
But in meetings with his national security advisers and after a series of intelligence briefings, Trump said he was considering holding off on strikes, said the people, who, like others interviewed for this story, spoke on condition of anonymity.
He has also indicated sympathy for allies in the region who have asked him not to return to a full-fledged war.
"I could end it immediately, but at the request of the nations that I am looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly," Trump told sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday.

Mohammed al-Shami's family learned of his death on 30 October, more than a month after it happened, and has received no explanation of the cause or circumstances.

"Our colleague must be laid to rest in a dignified manner, in accordance with the wishes of his family – which was denied contact with him for two years while he was in detention," said Volker Turk, the UN high commissioner for human rights.

"Do not allow Mohammed to die twice: once when he was taken from his family and disappeared, and again when the truth about his fate is allowed to disappear from the world," the statement said.
More than 70 UN employees and dozens of humanitarian workers remain in detention in Yemen.
Turk's office said a video circulating this week appeared to show one of them "confessing", and voiced fears that the detainees may be subjected to torture or ill-treatment.

Turkey and Qatar have signed a mutual defence agreement in Istanbul on Friday, in what is the latest military pact between Ankara and other Muslim states.
The defence agreement was one of five agreed between Turkey and Qatar, as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
A statement by the Turkish president's office said that Friday's mutual defence agreement with Qatar "would add another dimension to our brotherhood".
Erdogan said Turkey and Qatar’s cooperation in the defence industry would continue to grow, according to the statement.
Turkey and Qatar have had several defence agrements since 2017, including the hosting of Turkish troops in Doha, but the new deal obliged both countries to come to the other's defence.
In August this year, Turkey signed a defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, known as the Mecca Agreement.
Last week, the Turkish parliament passed a law approving the Mecca defence pact early on Friday, completing a crucial stage in the legal process.
The move will allow the deployment of Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia, which is currently at war with Yemen's Houthis.
In October, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that any deployment to Saudi Arabia would be defensive in nature and that Turkish forces would not operate in Yemen.
